audit_record.flaw_origin: The complete vulnerable mechanism originated in the single-parent feature commit 6ae088a658077a2f11a83ded6ac53c0dbddefd38: it created core/webhook.go, added the network listener and /hook handler, defined the JSON exec field, made an empty token authenticate successfully, passed exec to sh -c, wired the server into main, and documented an empty token as disabling authentication. This is the smallest repository-visible BIC, not the later shell-helper refactor.
audit_record.reasoning: The vulnerability is a composed trust-boundary failure, not merely the existence of a shell API. With webhook.enabled true, the BIC binds the webhook listener to every interface; an omitted token causes authenticate to approve every caller; handleHook accepts a caller-provided exec action; and executeShell supplies that string as the shell program. A usable request also needs a session key whose platform context can be reconstructed, and possibly a project selector, but neither substitutes for authentication. The 6ae088a commit introduced all of these pieces at once and even added a test requiring empty-token authentication to pass. Its immediate parent has no core/webhook.go or equivalent webhook-exec route, so absence is tree-proven. Pickaxe history finds no earlier writer, while the only later sink change is a behavior-preserving helper refactor. Tag membership brackets introduction between v1.2.2-beta.1 and v1.2.2-beta.2 and confirms persistence through the advisory's v1.4.1 boundary. There is no remediation commit: both the latest stable tag and audited HEAD retain the bypass and shell dispatch, so null fix fields are justified and unpatched status is recorded. Finally, the smallest BIC's own commit object explicitly says `generated by llmgit` and credits Claude as co-author. Since that AI-marked object is the first writer of the flawed authentication-plus-exec design, the causal verdict is AI_ROOT_CAUSE.
audit_record.remaining_gap: The vulnerability remains unpatched in every fetched ref of the validated clone through HEAD 80713167d17b3f2a3906efc3b14b3acab39766e4 and v1.5.1-beta.1; therefore no fix SHA or direct-fix SHA exists to audit. A future remediation commit and patched release boundary are the only outstanding lifecycle facts.

causal_chain.bug_semantics: An authenticated DatoCMS user could supply an absolute or protocol-relative external URL in the visual inspector's path query parameter. ContentLinkContext copied that value unchanged into iframeState.path, and UI then placed it unchanged in the redirect parameter of the configured enableDraftModeUrl. When the draft-mode endpoint followed redirect, the inspector iframe could be navigated to an attacker-chosen origin, bypassing the configured frontend-origin restriction.
causal_chain.flaw_origin: The Visual Editing feature was introduced with both ends of the unsafe data flow in one commit: web-previews/src/entrypoints/Inspector/ContentLinkContext/index.tsx accepted ctx.location.search path without origin validation, while web-previews/src/entrypoints/Inspector/UI/index.tsx forwarded iframeState.path to the draft-mode redirect parameter without validating it at the iframe sink.

causal_chain.bug_semantics: For a window drawable, do_get_buffers allocated only count + 1 DRI2BufferPtr slots, filled count client-requested slots, and then used arithmetic attachment counters to decide whether to append implicit front buffers. With at least two DRI2BufferBackLeft requests and one DRI2BufferFrontLeft request, need_real_front remained positive even though FrontLeft was already present, so a redundant real-front pointer was appended at buffers[count]. The FrontLeft request also made need_fake_front positive, so the fake-front pointer was then written at buffers[count + 1], one pointer beyond the heap allocation. The DRI2GetBuffers and DRI2GetBuffersWithFormat request paths both called this helper, allowing a local X client to crash the server or potentially escalate privileges when it ran as root.
causal_chain.flaw_origin: Commit ff6c7764c2909e4126403b7211faa6c58556b341 replaced the parent's bulk CreateBuffers path with per-attachment allocation and introduced need_real_front++/-- alongside the existing fake-front accounting, while retaining an allocation sized for only one implicit attachment. The parent could append at most one fake front and therefore respected its count + 1 capacity; the new combination could append both a redundant real front and a fake front. Treating attachment presence as signed counts rather than boolean presence broke the allocation invariant.

causal_chain.bug_semantics: An X client can send XkbSetMap with a non-canonical key type whose one-byte numLevels is as large as 255. CheckKeyTypes accepted every positive value and stored it even though downstream code assumes at most XkbMaxShiftLevel (63). A later core ChangeKeyboardMapping reaches XkbUpdateKeyTypesFromCore and XkbKeyTypesForCoreSymbols, where the tainted level count becomes groupsWidth and XKB_OFFSET(g,l) indexes a 252-entry XkbMaxSymsPerKey stack buffer; at width 255 the maximum index is 1019. The same oversized key geometry can also make XkbChangeTypesOfKey copy excessive symbols and actions into its fixed oldSyms and oldActs stack arrays, yielding three client-triggerable stack overflows and possible crash or privilege escalation when the server is privileged.
causal_chain.flaw_origin: The causal mechanism is the combination of CheckKeyTypes validating only numLevels >= 1 and the XKB conversion/resizing paths using fixed XkbMaxShiftLevel * XkbNumKbdGroups stack arrays without independently bounding stored non-canonical type widths. All of those lines already appear in the repository's 2003 R6.6 vendor baseline import, whose immediate parent contains no xkb tree. That 609-file baseline aggregate imported pre-existing X11/XFree86 code rather than authoring the mechanism, so the smallest original change and its parent are beyond this Git history. The 2025 CVE-2025-26597 fix changed only the nGroups == 0 action-resize path and did not introduce this excessive-numLevels path.

causal_chain.bug_semantics: With federation enabled, NodeBB authenticated the HTTP-signature key against the ActivityPub activity actor and required object.id to have that actor's origin, but did not bind object.attributedTo to the authenticated actor. A remote actor could therefore send a signed Create whose object.id was on the attacker's origin but whose attributedTo was a bare local numeric uid such as 1. The inbound mock copied attributedTo into the post/message uid; actors.assert filtered numeric identifiers out and its false result was ignored, after which topic or chat persistence treated the attacker-chosen local uid as the author.
causal_chain.flaw_origin: Commit f74775365a57262488434c920c7b805608b761c7 first made the unsafe attribution mapping remotely exploitable: it added inbox.create, took only req.body.object for authorship, passed the untrusted object through activitypub.mocks.post, and persisted the resulting postData without comparing attributedTo to the authenticated req.body.actor. The unsafe mocks.post assignment had been prepared in f1e5e5a0ad4cc6d5a02bf9bc952e524fe2f58458 and moved by 06e1583461f034d68c8c3c6d69547b06ad6ab3b5, but f74775365a57262488434c920c7b805608b761c7 is the smallest commit that connected it to the inbound Create attack surface and made the remote post-forgery path real.

`git show f74775365a57262488434c920c7b805608b761c7 -- src/activitypub/inbox.js` adds inbox.create: it reads object from req.body, calls activitypub.mocks.post(object), and sends postData to activitypub.notes.assert without reading or comparing the authenticated actor. The commit has one parent, so it is neither a merge nor a squash aggregate.

Direct parent-tree verification with `git grep -n 'inbox.create = async' 756548520401e1f920d358ad61ec1f28451173d5 -- src/activitypub/inbox.js` returned no match. The parent already contained the generic mock, but no inbound Create handler connected a remote signed activity to that mock-and-persist path; the f74775365a57262488434c920c7b805608b761c7 diff is the minimal enabling change.

At v4.13.2, src/middleware/activitypub.js verifies the HTTP signature, derives req.uid from keyId, checks key ownership against req.body.actor, and checks actor hostname against object.id hostname, but never checks object.attributedTo. src/activitypub/inbox.js create passes object to notes.assert; src/activitypub/mocks.js maps attributedTo to uid, calls actors.assert(uid) without checking its return, and returns uid in the persistence payload; src/activitypub/actors.js explicitly filters numeric ids; src/activitypub/notes.js ultimately calls topics.post with authorId or messaging.sendMessage with payload.uid.

History cross-checks show the precursor assignment `attributedTo: uid` originated in f1e5e5a0ad4cc6d5a02bf9bc952e524fe2f58458, was only moved by refactor 06e1583461f034d68c8c3c6d69547b06ad6ab3b5, and became remotely reachable in f74775365a57262488434c920c7b805608b761c7. The unsafe mocks.post assignment had been prepared in f1e5e5a0ad4cc6d5a02bf9bc952e524fe2f58458 and moved by 06e1583461f034d68c8c3c6d69547b06ad6ab3b5, but f74775365a57262488434c920c7b805608b761c7 is the smallest commit that connected it to the inbound Create attack surface and made the remote post-forgery path real.
audit_record.reasoning: The causal split matters. f1e5e5a0ad4cc6d5a02bf9bc952e524fe2f58458 created a generic remote-note mock that trusted attributedTo, but its existence alone did not provide the advisory's unauthenticated remote inbox attack. f74775365a57262488434c920c7b805608b761c7 is the first complete vulnerable state: it added the signed inbound Create handler and connected the untrusted object to that mock and persistence while omitting the authenticated actor from the author decision. Its immediate parent has no inbox.create handler, so the remote path is directly absent there. causal_chain.bug_semantics: During ListFonts/ListFontsWithInfo alias resolution, libXfont2 can return a fonts.alias target up to MAXFONTNAMELEN (1024) bytes, but the server used 256-byte tmp_pattern and LFWIstateRec.pattern buffers and copied resolvedlen/namelen bytes into them without first checking either length. A local client able to add a crafted font directory with SetFontPath and request the alias can therefore drive a 257-1023 byte target through the font provider and overflow stack-resident state, causing a crash or potentially privilege escalation when the server is privileged.
causal_chain.flaw_origin: The first xserver repository commit containing the mechanism, the R6.6 baseline import, simultaneously added #define XLFDMAXFONTNAMELEN 256 in include/closestr.h and the unchecked memmove(tmp_pattern, resolved, resolvedlen) and memmove(c->current.pattern, name, namelen) alias paths in dix/dixfonts.c. Its immediate parent contains neither file. Later formatting, memmove-to-memcpy, and libXfont2 API migration commits preserved rather than originated the size mismatch and unchecked length-controlled writes.

causal_chain.bug_semantics: The unauthenticated /cgi-bin/api.values.get handler in the Grandstream GXP1600 firmware's 32-bit ARM /app/bin/gs_web binary parses the attacker-controlled request parameter as colon-delimited identifiers and copies each non-colon byte into a 64-byte stack buffer without checking the identifier length. An identifier longer than 63 bytes writes beyond that buffer, and repeated colon-delimited identifiers let an attacker place multiple terminating NUL bytes, overwrite saved registers including PC, build a ROP chain, and invoke system() as root.
causal_chain.flaw_origin: The flawed bounds-free identifier-copy loop belongs to Grandstream's proprietary GXP1600 firmware, not rapid7/metasploit-framework. Its source and version-control history are not public, so the exact introducing source commit is beyond the public-history boundary. Metasploit commit 08efa9cd16f254bfc8f2f4cee0550f3a851e0aa5 merely added an exploit for the already-existing device flaw after fixed firmware 1.0.7.81 had been released; it did not write the vulnerable /app/bin/gs_web code.

It documents PC control and the repeated-colon/NUL technique used to construct a ROP chain and execute commands as root.

The disclosure tested vulnerable firmware 1.0.7.79 and says users must upgrade to 1.0.7.81 or above. Its timeline records that Grandstream made 1.0.7.81 available, reaffirmed the issue resolved in that release, and that Rapid7 independently verified remediation by reverse engineering the public firmware. This is binary verification, not a public source commit.

Grandstream's release notes (https://firmware.grandstream.com/Release_Note_GXP16xx_1.0.7.81.pdf) list 1.0.7.81 for all six affected models, date it 2026-01-30, and include 'Fixed some security vulnerabilities.' The preceding 1.0.7.80 is dated 2025-12-31. This parent-tree result applies only to the exploit client and cannot establish absence of the firmware flaw.

causal_chain.bug_semantics: A remote Bluetooth device can supply an EIR name element whose field_len is 254, making eir_parse pass data_len 253 to name2utf8. On the non-UTF-8 conversion path, name2utf8 used strncpy with that attacker-controlled length to copy into utf8_name[HCI_MAX_NAME_LENGTH + 2]. HCI_MAX_NAME_LENGTH is 248, so the 250-byte stack array is overrun by three bytes; the missing terminator can also make the subsequent stripping and duplication read beyond the array. Discovery therefore permits a radio-adjacent unauthenticated peer to crash bluetoothd and potentially corrupt control data.
causal_chain.flaw_origin: Commit 155fa21473ada6d3e7773175186badd4bc0fde22 first added src/eir.c:name2utf8 and coupled the fixed 250-byte utf8_name array to strncpy(..., len), where len is derived from the untrusted EIR element length and can be 253. Although the subject calls the change a move, the removed src/event.c code copied at the fixed MGMT_MAX_NAME_LENGTH bound, while the newly added EIR helper introduced the attacker-length copy; it is therefore the smallest causal introducer rather than a pure move. Later commit 218db700f49370bc07ce1e6d609d28d846470d99 changed character conversion but retained the already-vulnerable array and copy.

audit_record.ai_marker: absent: the raw commit object for 155fa21473ada6d3e7773175186badd4bc0fde22 names Johan Hedberg <johan.hedberg@intel.com> as both author and committer and contains only the subject 'core: Move UTF-8 validation of device names into eir.c'; it has no Co-Authored-By, Generated-with, Assisted-by, bot identity, or other AI trailer/marker.

causal_chain.bug_semantics: When the opt-in Management API is enabled with its token left empty, its authentication middleware treats the empty secret as successful authentication. The server listens on all interfaces at port 9820, and an unauthenticated remote POST to /api/v1/cron can copy attacker-controlled JSON exec text into a persisted CronJob. The cron scheduler identifies a nonempty Exec as a shell job and ultimately runs that text through the configured shell, so the attacker obtains command execution when the job fires; later code also added an immediate /api/v1/cron/{id}/exec trigger, but that was not necessary for the original scheduled-execution path.
causal_chain.flaw_origin: The vulnerable trust-boundary crossing was created in one change: c2681402a7686294174a263e31245a52d4fea380 added the network-facing Management API, deliberately made authenticate return true for an empty token, registered the cron endpoints behind that fail-open middleware, and assigned untrusted req.Exec directly to CronJob.Exec. The shell-capable CronJob and its sh -c execution sink already existed in the parent; c2681402 is the smallest commit that made that sink reachable from an unauthenticated remote management request.

causal_chain.bug_semantics: The unauthenticated GET /_instatic/hole/<nodeId> handler treats the attacker-controlled u parameter as the originating page URL and uses its path, slug, and query to render a shared hole, but its process-wide cache key contains only nodeId, publish version, and u's normalized inner query. Because u's pathname is content-varying but absent from the key, an attacker can render route-dependent HTML for a chosen pathname into the slot later used by a legitimate request with the same nodeId, version, and query.
causal_chain.flaw_origin: Commit f066a8838e49ba211250c56c2955a25689e5e7ca first forwarded location.pathname + location.search as u, parsed u into pageUrl, exposed pageUrl-derived route.path and route.slug to rendering and request-dependent loop sources, and simultaneously keyed shared-hole responses as v=<version>&normalizeQuery(pageUrl.searchParams), omitting the content-varying pageUrl pathname. The older hole cache existed, but its parent did not accept u or render from an attacker-selected page URL, so it did not contain this poisoning mechanism.

causal_chain.bug_semantics: When proxy memory is enabled, the proxy treats the caller-controlled x-headroom-user-id header as the authoritative memory partition key without authenticating or otherwise binding that value to the caller. A remote client can select a victim identifier, causing memory search results to be injected into the attacker's LLM context and memory tool operations to read, create, update, or delete records in the victim's partition; this is a CWE-639 confidentiality and integrity failure.
causal_chain.flaw_origin: Commit da743418584725e8b9c3315dc1aea7cf5e949192 first integrated persistent memory into the network proxy and wrote memory_user_id = headers.get("x-headroom-user-id") in headroom/proxy/server.py, then passed that untrusted value directly to search_and_format_context and handle_memory_tool_calls. The pre-existing reference docker-compose configuration already bound the proxy to 0.0.0.0 and published port 8787, and the BIC added no caller authentication or identity binding, so the new partition selector was remotely attacker-controlled in the shipped deployment model.

causal_chain.bug_semantics: In SPIP 4.4.20, analyse_resultat_skel() examined the inner text of each PHP block with an anchored header() regular expression that mistakenly retained PCRE's multiline modifier. Because ^ and $ therefore matched individual lines rather than the whole PHP block, an unauthenticated attacker could inject a newline-delimited header("X-Spip-Filtre: intval|_request|system") line into generated template code. SPIP extracted that attacker-selected filter chain, intval reduced the body to the key 0, _request read attacker-controlled POST parameter 0, and system executed it, yielding pre-authentication remote code execution.
causal_chain.flaw_origin: The vulnerable product code is in the upstream spip/ecrire repository, not in the bundled rapid7/metasploit-framework reference. Commit d369f5a49c3593f18b1c81fc3a3051bd0bed1e1d rewrote public/composer.php to collect individual PHP blocks and first added the vulnerable /^...$/ims match over each block's innerHtml. Its immediate parent used a materially different whole-page preg_match_all implementation and did not contain this vulnerable collector-plus-multiline-anchors mechanism. Rapid7 commit b16eca819abb8f1401f21d115e71e3dfc67b847c only added an exploit module and documentation after the SPIP flaw existed; it neither introduced nor fixed SPIP.

causal_chain.bug_semantics: With OAuth enabled behind a TLS-terminating reverse proxy, Temporal UI Server created browser authentication cookies with Secure set from c.Request().TLS, which describes only the proxy-to-server hop. When that hop was HTTP, the access-token user cookies (and later refresh-token cookies when an IdP issued one) lacked Secure even though the browser used HTTPS. An attacker who could additionally steer the UI hostname, defeat HTTPS, serve it over HTTP, and observe a later same-site plaintext request could recover and replay the live credential.
causal_chain.flaw_origin: The original ui-server commit replaced always-Secure server-side session cookies with browser-resident user0/userN cookies containing the OAuth access token and set each cookie's Secure field to c.Request().TLS != nil. That made a deployment-internal transport property control a browser-facing cookie security boundary. The monorepo later imported this already-flawed code, and later refresh/session work reused the same derivation; neither the import nor those extensions are the first root-cause commit.

causal_chain.bug_semantics: A template-controlled reverse range such as (100000000..1) makes evalRangeToken charge high - low + 1, a large negative count. Limiter.use accepted that negative count and added it to its cumulative base, creating artificial budget credit. Later append/replace operations could therefore exceed the configured memoryLimit; flattening the resulting large V8 cons-string could terminate the Node.js process, producing denial of service.
causal_chain.flaw_origin: Commit 2af297f81ac465feb3277ba7b92f7236409370b0 added ctx.memoryLimit.use(high - low + 1) to src/render/expression.ts without constraining the charge to a non-negative range size. The pre-existing Limiter.use implementation accepted and accumulated signed counts, so this new attacker-controlled negative callsite completed the underflow/budget-bypass mechanism. Reverse ranges themselves return an empty array because range(start, stop) loops only while start < stop, making the negative charge pure budget credit rather than a matching allocation.

causal_chain.bug_semantics: LiquidJS promised to bound each render with renderLimit, but Render.renderTemplates checked elapsed time only inside its loop over template nodes. An empty for or tablerow body parses to an empty templates array, so every attacker-controlled collection iteration calls renderTemplates([]), executes no check, and consumes CPU linearly up to the separate memoryLimit while bypassing the configured wall-clock budget.
causal_chain.flaw_origin: Commit e443068cb9281883ff0fe9f755a15f52ada4e7e2 introduced the renderLimit feature and its first enforcement point as ctx.renderLimit.check(performance.now()) inside for (const tpl of templates). The existing for and tablerow tags could pass an empty body array once per collection element, so placing the new security check exclusively inside the zero-trip inner loop created the bypass at the moment the guard was introduced.

causal_chain.bug_semantics: The default-registered strip_html filter applied one global regular expression containing unbounded lazy script, style, comment, and generic-tag alternatives directly to attacker-controlled template data. On many opener tokens without a matching closer, V8 retries an alternative at each '<' and scans the remaining suffix looking for the absent terminator, producing quadratic work on the single Node.js event-loop thread. memoryLimit did not bound that CPU work because it charged only the input string length before String.replace ran.
causal_chain.flaw_origin: Commit 8e9e10fdb4c7f00ffa3997d3e2c0a0bfa48ce887 replaced the prior simple tag regex in filters.js with the Ruby-Liquid-compatible /<script.*?<\/script>|<!--.*?-->|<style.*?<\/style>|<.*?>/g expression. That functional-parity change first introduced the unbounded lazy alternatives and therefore the vulnerable repeated-suffix search; later moves and expansions preserved or broadened the same mechanism rather than originating it.

causal_chain.bug_semantics: LiquidJS treated a lexically resolved pathname under a configured template root as proof that the file ultimately opened was under that root. Node's file APIs then followed symlinks, so an attacker-controlled symlink located inside a trusted partials/layouts/root directory could target any readable file outside the directory; include, render, or layout would parse and render the external target.
causal_chain.flaw_origin: Commit 8fbbec089fa4e3db4bec47462b1c08dd65c36648 first introduced filesystem-backed template loading and the include tag. Its index.js handleCache() resolved the requested name with path.resolve(this.options.root, filepath) and immediately passed that non-canonical pathname to fs.readFileSync(), while tags/include.js routed an evaluated include name into handleCache(). That is the first complete path-check/path-construction-to-file-open mechanism that follows an in-root symlink without validating the target; later Loader.withinDir(), FS.contains(), file moves, and separate partials/layouts roots preserved or re-expressed the same flaw rather than introducing it.

causal_chain.bug_semantics: LiquidJS strip_html treated its output as tag-stripped text, but the generic-tag alternative <.*?> used JavaScript dot without dotAll, so it could not consume CR or LF inside angle brackets. Browsers accept those line terminators as whitespace between a tag name and attributes; consequently an attacker-controlled value such as <img\nsrc=x\nonerror=alert(1)> survived strip_html and became executable HTML/XSS when rendered without a separate escaping step.
causal_chain.flaw_origin: Commit 8e9e10fdb4c7f00ffa3997d3e2c0a0bfa48ce887 replaced the older tag-name-only strip_html regex in filters.js with a Ruby-Liquid-style alternation whose new generic branch was <.*?>. That one-line change first wrote the exact vulnerable construct: JavaScript '.' stops at CR/LF while browsers continue parsing the tag. Later moves and refactors preserved it. Commit 42d25902e855d3c06d5ead071bf55604f495c205 made script, style, and comment alternatives multiline-safe with [\s\S] but retained <.*?>; it sharpened the inconsistency described by the advisory but is not the BIC because the flawed generic branch already existed in its parent.

causal_chain.bug_semantics: Preact distinguishes genuine VNodes by giving them an own constructor value of undefined. In the affected client renderer, the gate became `if (newVNode.constructor != UNDEFINED) return NULL`; JavaScript loose equality treats null and undefined as equal, so a JSON-parsed attacker object shaped as a VNode and carrying `constructor: null` passes the gate. If an application passes that unsanitized object into the render tree, Preact consumes its attacker-controlled type and props as a VNode and can inject HTML, with script execution possible where CSP or other defenses do not stop it. The companion loose `childVNode.constructor == UNDEFINED` check also admits null as the VNode sentinel in child processing. The server-side preact-render-to-string path was not affected.

Its second member 7ed5aeb0246305e3b42e314c1a59bcaa405e6a8c restored three unrelated strict comparisons but retained both vulnerable changes; GitHub then squash-merged the resulting tree as a69aada2799626d3afbfc1eb6550611ca2444a4d. In the default state, SrsSecurity::check returns success immediately when security.enabled is false, so the publish path has no mandatory authentication boundary.

Its immediate parent only handled releaseStream/FCPublish/createStream and returned before consuming or accepting publish. Commit 75f2607685814b86ad030df703834cf06f91447f later added optional vhost allow/deny security with a false default and an explicit allow-all bypass, preserving rather than originating the already unauthenticated publish behavior.

causal_chain.bug_semantics: The manage-downloads admin deletion handler accepted attacker-controlled POST fields `file` and `file_name` independently of the integer `file_id`; when `unlinkfile=1`, it concatenated the configured download directory with `file` and passed the result to `unlink()`. Neither the original `trim()` nor the later `sanitize_text_field()` removes `../` segments or proves containment, so an authenticated administrator holding the normal delete nonce could alter the hidden `file` field and delete an arbitrary server file outside the download directory. Deleting a critical file such as wp-config.php can cause denial of service and can enable follow-on site compromise/RCE.
causal_chain.flaw_origin: The vulnerable trust boundary was present in the first public upstream source revision, WordPress Plugin SVN r7446 (2007-01-21): `trunk/downloadmanager/download-manager.php` read `$_POST['file']` and used it in `unlink($file_path.'/'.$file)` rather than deriving the path from the database row selected by `file_id`. Later renames, SVN-to-Git deployment, sanitization, and formatting preserved that mechanism. Git commit d3470a8971d9043438c8aad281cf37d14fefa208 fixed the root cause by accepting only `file_id`, reloading the downloads-table row, and unlinking the stored `$file->file` value.

causal_chain.bug_semantics: An authenticated WordPress administrator can submit a download_path such as WP_CONTENT_DIR . '/../..'. The validation compares the uncanonicalized string prefix with WP_CONTENT_DIR, so the traversal-bearing string passes even though filesystem resolution escapes wp-content. causal_chain.bug_semantics: An attacker can place OSC/CSI control bytes in a filesystem entry name. causal_chain.bug_semantics: An authenticated backend user with backend.manage_editor could save attacker-controlled LESS in Editor Settings -> Markup Styles. EditorSetting::compileCss() concatenated html_custom_styles into a .fr-view rule and returned Less_Parser output; LESS escaped-string syntax such as ~"</style><script>alert(1)</script><style>" preserved HTML delimiters. After the output-side strip_tags() call was removed, _custom_styles.php embedded that compiled string verbatim inside a <style> element used by the normal and authentication backend layouts, allowing stored CSS to terminate the style element and execute script when another backend user loaded a page.
causal_chain.flaw_origin: Commit c9dab67bc819b791df8432a898dd976f19388a87 changed only the exception path to e($ex->getMessage()) in EditorSetting::renderCss(), but simultaneously replaced <?= strip_tags(EditorSetting::renderCss()) ?> with the raw <?= EditorSetting::renderCss() ?> sink in modules/backend/layouts/_custom_styles.php. Escaping exception text did not sanitize successfully compiled, attacker-controlled LESS output, so this commit removed the defense from the successful compilation path without replacing it.

causal_chain.bug_semantics: A backend user holding backend.manage_branding can store attacker-controlled LESS in Settings -> Customize Backend -> Styles. BrandSetting::compileCss() concatenates custom_css into the LESS input; LESS escape syntax such as ~"</style><script>alert(1)</script><style>" preserves HTML delimiter and script text in the compiled result. BrandSetting::renderCss() returned that result without HTML sanitization, and modules/backend/layouts/_custom_styles.php echoed it inside a <style> element on backend pages, so the stored </style> breakout executes script for backend viewers.
causal_chain.flaw_origin: Commit 1203043a457dee3c298d7dd54289a866234cbb74 first changed BrandSettings.php from parsing only the bundled custom.less file to parsing that file concatenated with self::get('custom_css'), while the compiled output was persisted/rendered without stripping HTML tags. The immediate parent already had the custom_css settings field and the style sink, but did not feed custom_css into the compiler, so this one-line data-flow addition is the smallest real BIC rather than later cache, rename, refactor, or error-handling commits.

causal_chain.bug_semantics: The CMS controller admitted a backend user possessing any one CMS Theme Editor permission, but its AJAX handlers trusted the request-controlled template type and did not re-check the permission mapped to that type. A pages-only user could therefore open, create, save, delete, commit, or reset partials, layouts, content, or assets by crafting the handler parameters. The constructor also registered every template widget, including AssetList, for every admitted CMS user; AssetList's upload path processed a file without first binding the request to the active theme, so a user without cms.manage_assets could reach an unauthorized upload into the active theme's assets.
causal_chain.flaw_origin: Single-parent commit 71a5dd67ab9e0d0da7caabd3fb5aaa3d86bb45e5 introduced the exploitable design as new code: modules/cms/controllers/Index.php used the section-wide cms.* gate, instantiated every TemplateList and AssetList unconditionally, and dispatched request-supplied type values into load/create/save/delete operations without a type-specific authorization check. The same commit introduced AssetList.php with constructor-time checkUploadPostback() upload processing and no validateRequestTheme() call in that upload path, while expanding modules/cms/ServiceProvider.php to register distinct cms.manage_content/assets/pages/layouts permissions. Its parent had only a skeletal CMS ServiceProvider and had neither Index.php nor AssetList.php, so the permission boundary and bypass surface first coexist in this commit.

causal_chain.bug_semantics: An authenticated backend user could submit the self-service account save handler with an attacker-chosen form_context such as update. FormController trusted that POST value over the server-selected myaccount context, so Users::formExtendFields treated the request as an administrative user form and admitted role, individual-permission, and superuser-related fields into the form widget's save data. The handler still selected the attacker's own User model, allowing protected authorization attributes to be mass-updated and the account to gain higher backend privileges.
causal_chain.flaw_origin: Commit 94a4ccb6abccd025e7e201590999061574ffdeb9 made the Users controller's self-service mysettings action unrestricted by setting requiredPermissions to null. That small authorization change was the first point at which ordinary authenticated backend users could reach the already-existing unsafe composition of mysettings_onSave and POST-controlled FormController context selection; its parent still required backend.manage_users for the controller, so the low-privilege attack path was absent there.

causal_chain.bug_semantics: ScpClient.Download(string, DirectoryInfo) starts a recursive SCP receive and trusts the filename captured from each server-controlled C (file) or D (directory) protocol record. It joins that unvalidated value to the current local download directory and then creates the directory or opens the file for writing. A malicious, compromised, or MITM server can therefore supply ../ components (and, after the later Path.Combine form, rooted paths) to escape the caller's destination and create or overwrite any path writable by the client process. Exploitation requires the victim to initiate a recursive directory download from the attacker-controlled endpoint.
causal_chain.flaw_origin: Commit d96c93abb2f9409281bfb12d2da8622470a4b3e3 first added ScpClient and its recursive directory-download implementation. In Renci.SshClient/Renci.SshNet/ScpClient.NET.cs it parsed arbitrary remote C/D record names and used them directly in local directory creation and FileInfo construction without requiring a single safe path component. causal_chain.bug_semantics: A deserialization gadget carrier that performs JavaBeans property reads, most notably a collection sorted by Apache Commons BeanUtils BeanComparator, can treat the no-argument JDBC methods getConnection() and getPooledConnection() as readable properties named connection and pooledConnection. If an attacker-controlled serialized c3p0 DataSource or ConnectionPoolDataSource is configured to reach a susceptible JDBC driver, the property read invokes that driver-facing method during deserialization and can trigger the driver's dangerous behavior.

causal_chain.bug_semantics: Before 0.12.0, c3p0 represented the writable JavaBean property userOverridesAsString as 'HexAsciiSerializedMap[' plus hex-encoded Java serialization bytes. C3P0ImplUtils.parseUserOverridesAsString() stripped that wrapper, hex-decoded attacker-controlled bytes, and passed them to SerializableUtils.fromByteArray() without an allowlist. WrapperConnectionPoolDataSource invoked this parser from its vetoable-change listener whenever the property was reset, and ComboPooledDataSource exported the property through its javax.naming.Reference. An attacker able to supply a crafted property value directly, through a serialized ConnectionPoolDataSource, or through a JNDI Reference could therefore trigger gadget deserialization. In combination with the dependency's then-ungated indirect JNDI Reference/factoryClassLocation handling, this could download and execute attacker code; independently, deserializing arbitrary objects from a writable bean string was unsafe.
causal_chain.flaw_origin: The vulnerable mechanism first appears in the preserved public tree at e11fd1340644747977fa34bc3377704223b6ccb4, the c3p0-0.9.1-pre5 source-release snapshot import. That snapshot added C3P0ImplUtils.createUserOverridesAsString()/parseUserOverridesAsString(), the WrapperConnectionPoolDataSource listener that calls the parser, the constrained generated property, and ComboPooledDataSource's Reference exposure. Its parent 15b53cfce6ed1fb0a46fd6597c2b2e4470e6f8c9 (c3p0-0.9.0.4) has none of those identifiers. However, e11fd1340644747977fa34bc3377704223b6ccb4 is a 270-file import of a SourceForge release ZIP rather than the atomic changeset that authored the flawed mechanism, so the protocol forbids treating it as the BIC.

causal_chain.bug_semantics: An attacker-controlled Typebot imported from JSON could retain a Script block whose content the preview API returned as a client-side action. @typebot.io/js then compiled that untrusted content with Function/AsyncFunction directly in the authenticated builder page. Code run there could make same-origin fetch requests with the victim's session, enumerate the victim's user/workspace credentials, receive decrypted credential data from credentials.getCredentials, and exfiltrate API keys, OAuth tokens, and passwords. The workspace form of getCredentials also authorized the supplied workspace but, at the vulnerable snapshot, did not bind the requested credential ID to that workspace.
causal_chain.flaw_origin: The single member commit behind PR #194 introduced all three causal pieces together: file import accepted JSON.parse(fileContent) without marking executable blocks untrusted, the viewer converted Script/Code block content into a codeToExecute client action, and the new @typebot.io/js executeCode implementation invoked Function on that content in the page context. It supplied neither a trust boundary for imported bots nor a sandbox/credentialless execution context.

causal_chain.bug_semantics: Attacker-controlled template expressions were evaluated as Python with a live rendering context. In the 0.1.x interpolation path, `{{ x.__class__.__mro__[1].__subclasses__() }}` passed a context-rooted dotted expression to raw `eval`; an empty globals dictionary is not a sandbox, because Python attribute traversal from any ordinary context object reaches the process object graph and can recover classes, module globals, and command-execution primitives. The 0.2.0-alpha rewrite retained the defect: `ExpressionEvaluator` either walked arbitrary attributes/methods or routed expressions containing an operator to `safe_eval`, which called raw `eval` with only `__builtins__` emptied. Commit 62c95c472fbd9ca5630a989ddec9d8899256726a replaced those paths with an AST interpreter that rejects underscore-prefixed attributes and restricts callable methods/builtins.

causal_chain.bug_semantics: getFilenameFromUrl accepts a decoded request pathname when it merely starts with the configured publicPath pathname, rejects dot-dot only when UP_PATH_REGEXP sees `..` as a complete path segment, and then slices the accepted string at publicPathPathname.length before passing the suffix to path.join(outputPath, ...). With a non-slash-terminated publicPath `/assets`, `/assets../.env` passes the prefix check and guard because `..` is embedded in the `assets..` segment, but the slice produces `../.env`, so path.join resolves one directory above outputPath. Disclosure requires the physical filesystem (writeToDisk or a custom outputFileSystem); the default memfs and default publicPath `auto`/`/` do not expose this path, and URL normalization limits this bypass to one parent directory.

causal_chain.bug_semantics: An EventStream subscriber was authorized only at dashboard-subscription granularity, then placed in a global client registry. OnExecutionStarted, OnExecutionFinished, and OnOutputChunk iterated that registry and sent every execution event to every subscriber without applying acl.IsAllowedLogs for the recipient and action. The finished-event LogEntry included the command's accumulated Output, while OutputChunk exposed live bytes, so a low-privileged authenticated dashboard user could observe metadata and output for an action whose logs that user was not authorized to view.

causal_chain.bug_semantics: OliveTin's Logout RPC expired the browser's olivetin-sid-local cookie but did not revoke the corresponding SID in server-side SessionStorage. Authentication continued to resolve a replayed SID through GetUserSession until its roughly one-year expiry, so anyone retaining the old cookie remained authenticated after the user appeared to log out; the same design later also cleared the OAuth2 cookie without deleting its server-side state.

This is the smallest commit that first wrote the advisory's clear-client-cookie-only mechanism; later cookie/security edits preserved it until the fix.

causal_chain.bug_semantics: With saveLogs enabled, a caller authorized to execute an action can supply a nonempty, nonduplicate StartAction UniqueTrackingId containing slash and .. segments. OliveTin accepts that string, stores it as the log entry's ExecutionTrackingID, interpolates it into the .yaml and .log filenames, and passes those names to path.Join. path.Join cleans the traversal segments, so ioutil.WriteFile writes both files outside the configured log directories to attacker-selected paths writable by the OliveTin process.
causal_chain.flaw_origin: The existing API-to-executor path already accepted arbitrary client tracking strings. PR #300's sole member commit fe991045b5bd9c7fbe57bb83a12a56deca68ef06 first made that unsafe value filesystem-relevant by adding stepSaveLog, composing filenames from ExecutionTrackingID without validation or basename confinement, joining them to configured directories, and writing them. GitHub integrated that one-member commit as squash commit 8fd98874e2b62c693cf2ab086f6c006020507760 with the same tree; the squash aggregate is not used as the BIC.

causal_chain.bug_semantics: OliveTin authorizes action execution and log disclosure independently. A caller granted exec:true but logs:false could invoke StartActionAndWait or StartActionByGetAndWait; each handler waited for the execution, fetched its InternalLogEntry, converted it to the public LogEntry (including stdout/stderr/output and exit status), and returned it without applying IsAllowedLogs. The synchronous response therefore disclosed exactly the output that GetLogs and the other log-bearing paths were meant to withhold.
causal_chain.flaw_origin: The synchronous wait endpoints already existed when log visibility was not an independent ACL permission. The causal flaw began when PR #273's sole member commit 2338cd0cc8e1fe2a9729c58bf31fbfc5dc342feb introduced PermissionsList.Logs and IsAllowedLogs, and guarded GetLogs, but left both pre-existing synchronous response paths returning internalLogEntryToPb(...) unguarded. This created the exec:true/logs:false policy state while omitting enforcement on the two immediate-output paths. The member was squash-landed as db5de9be9793be65e2a77ab71656713f97bc779b; later refactors and file moves preserved the omission until the 2026 fix.

causal_chain.bug_semantics: The unauthenticated GET /images endpoint accepts an image source and sends the resulting bytes to Sharp. For SVG input, imageProcessor deliberately rasterizes at density 300 with limitInputPixels disabled and performs no structural bound on use-element shadow-tree depth or pattern-tile dimensions. A crafted SVG can therefore make the underlying SVG renderer consume unbounded CPU or memory until the application server, and potentially the host, is denied service.
causal_chain.flaw_origin: Commit 5ed5ba31913ae69d617089988aa4ffe8015d6143 first added packages/evershop/src/modules/cms/services/imageProcessor.ts and its unsafe SVG branch, including density: 300 and limitInputPixels: false, plus the request handler that passes attacker-selected src into the processor. Its immediate child a839543becedb75324a16c38194eb4c64ba5f635 registered that handler as public GET /images; the first affected release v2.1.0 contains both commits. The root-cause lines themselves originate in 5ed5ba31913ae69d617089988aa4ffe8015d6143, so the later route-enablement commit is lifecycle context rather than the BIC.

causal_chain.bug_semantics: The public GraphQL Query.order resolver accepts an attacker-controlled order UUID and loads the matching order without authenticating the caller or constraining the query to the caller's customer/session identity. An unauthenticated caller who obtains a valid UUID can therefore traverse the returned Order fields and nested resolvers to read customer email/name, billing and shipping addresses, purchased items, totals, payment state, and shipment data belonging to another customer.
causal_chain.flaw_origin: Commit 685f3baf290024133c45986100fc7296ee14c85e changed the order lookup from an integer order_id plus tokenPayload-derived customer_id/sid ownership predicates to a string UUID lookup alone: it deleted extraction of customerId and sid and deleted both ownership/session constraints, leaving query.where('uuid', '=', id). Later commits renamed the argument to uuid, moved the file, and replaced the base select helper, but preserved this authorization omission.

evidence: The assigned GitHub advisory GHSA-c73g-mx2w-cc93 / CVE-2025-12919 identifies src/modules/oms/graphql/types/Order/Order.resolvers.js, declares @evershop/evershop <= 2.1.0 vulnerable, and supplies no first_patched_version.

The linked public disclosure https://github.com/ictrun/Evershop-Order-leak/blob/main/README.md documents an unauthenticated POST to /api/graphql with order(uuid: $uuid) returning order/customer PII; its quoted vulnerable resolver performs getOrdersBaseQuery(), where uuid equals caller input, and load(pool), with no authorization predicate.

numactl git log 685f3baf290024133c45986100fc7296ee14c85e -L 8,18:packages/core/src/modules/checkout/graphql/types/Order/Order.resolvers.js traces the causal lines from the secure introduction in 44a884b59e51d29f5022aa5b482b6c12e56ebfaa through 685f3baf290024133c45986100fc7296ee14c85e. The latter is the first commit to delete `const { customerId, sid } = tokenPayload`, `andWhere('customer_id', '=', customerId)`, and `.or('sid', '=', sid)`, while adding the UUID-only predicate.

Direct tree comparison `git diff b398f43d4d2eedf39abf9e3658820941cbd4babd 685f3baf290024133c45986100fc7296ee14c85e -- packages/core/src/modules/checkout/graphql/types/Order/Order.{graphql,resolvers.js}` proves immediate-parent absence: the parent requires order_id plus customer_id or sid, whereas the BIC changes the schema argument from Int to String and leaves only `query.where('uuid', '=', id)`.

The BIC is a single-parent public commit (parent b398f43d4d2eedf39abf9e3658820941cbd4babd), not a merge, move, refactor, revert, or release commit. Although it is a broad 195-file change, the public graph exposes no smaller member commit; the vulnerable authorization deletion is directly present in its own diff, so there are no decomposed SHAs.

History checks corroborate the selection: `git log -S "query.andWhere('customer_id'" -- **/Order/Order.resolvers.js` and `git log -S "customerId, sid"` identify only the secure introduction 44a884b59e51d29f5022aa5b482b6c12e56ebfaa and removal 685f3baf290024133c45986100fc7296ee14c85e. Blame was used only as a lead; later commits 72d478a748e7994b46f7aecee9a849a9ef15db43 and 7a7fb5b089663bf86e47d8825ca64bb7fafce2b3 merely rename/restructure the already-unscoped lookup.

Version-boundary checks show `git tag --contains 685f3baf290024133c45986100fc7296ee14c85e` includes the first tagged release 1.0.0-rc.9, v1.0.0, every listed stable release through the advisory boundary v2.1.0, and later tags v2.1.1, v2.1.2, and v2.2.1. `git merge-base --is-ancestor` also succeeds for v2.1.0, so the BIC predates and is contained in the affected range.

No fix exists in reachable history. At both v2.1.0 (70a786fadcbd55f1641f0088189da4cfe44aa79c) and the latest reachable tag v2.2.1 (abfdabcacfc49ad0df1f262c34bc46af721f2537), packages/evershop/src/modules/oms/graphql/types/Order/Order.resolvers.js still resolves order(uuid) by getOrdersBaseQuery(), adds only `where('uuid', '=', uuid)`, and returns the loaded order. The later anonymous tracking-token page code does not constrain the public GraphQL resolver itself.

BIC-only AI inspection used the raw commit object, not PR text, branch names, later code, or a fix: `git cat-file -p 685f3baf290024133c45986100fc7296ee14c85e` shows a human GitHub noreply author/committer, identical timestamps/identity, and no trailers or bot marker. This supports NOT_AI independently of any later repository activity.
audit_record.flaw_origin: Commit 685f3baf290024133c45986100fc7296ee14c85e changed the order lookup from an integer order_id plus tokenPayload-derived customer_id/sid ownership predicates to a string UUID lookup alone: it deleted extraction of customerId and sid and deleted both ownership/session constraints, leaving query.where('uuid', '=', id). Later commits renamed the argument to uuid, moved the file, and replaced the base select helper, but preserved this authorization omission.
audit_record.reasoning: The vulnerability began as an authorization regression, not with the original GraphQL endpoint. Commit 44a884b59e51d29f5022aa5b482b6c12e56ebfaa initially loaded an order only when its numeric ID matched and either customer_id matched tokenPayload.customerId or sid matched tokenPayload.sid. The immediate parent of the selected BIC still has those constraints. Commit 685f3baf290024133c45986100fc7296ee14c85e deliberately converted the public argument to a string UUID and simultaneously removed both identity predicates, making possession of an order UUID sufficient. That exact removal is the smallest causally relevant public commit; subsequent parameter renames, module moves, ESM/TypeScript conversions, and query-helper refactors preserve rather than originate the flaw. The BIC predates 1.0.0-rc.9 and is an ancestor of the advisory's upper affected boundary v2.1.0. The advisory reports no patched version, and direct inspection shows the same unscoped resolver still present at v2.2.1, so fix_sha and direct_fix_sha are justified nulls rather than missing research. Finally, the only admissible AI evidence is the BIC commit object: it has a human author/committer and no AI/co-author/generated/bot trailer. Therefore the causal BIC is real and parent-verified, but has no commit-object AI signal, yielding NOT_AI.
audit_record.remaining_gap: The vulnerability remains unpatched in the reachable public history: there is no fix commit, direct-fix commit, or first patched version to record, and the latest inspected release v2.2.1 still exposes the UUID-only resolver.

causal_chain.bug_semantics: An attacker-controlled account value can be reflected by the REST error path in ExceptionMessage and the JSON response body. The account_rse_usage WebUI error callbacks passed the raw jqXHR.responseText through string concatenation to jQuery.html(), so the victim's browser parsed payload markup such as an img onerror handler in the Rucio WebUI origin instead of displaying it as text. A crafted link therefore executes script when an authenticated user opens it, exposing the WebUI token/session and permitting actions with the victim's authority.
causal_chain.flaw_origin: Commit 045193619da3087de74d77ec0f715ce57c1ed035 created lib/rucio/web/ui/static/account_rse_usage.js and, in both nested request error callbacks, wrote $("#results").html('<font color="red">' + jqXHR['responseText'] + '</font>'). That new page combined an attacker-influenced server response with an HTML parsing sink without encoding it; this is the concrete sink exercised by the advisory's account_rse_usage?account= payload.

audit_record.ai_marker: absent: the BIC commit object names Thomas Beermann <thomas.beermann@cern.ch> as both author and committer and contains only the subject '[RUCIO-640] add new account usage page + add human readable file sizes' plus Change-Id: I127ad60197cde1848035a1878b3369dec2f67c86; it has no Co-Authored-By, Generated-with, bot identity, or other AI marker.

causal_chain.bug_semantics: nltk.data.find() accepts a resource name that is supposed to remain beneath an NLTK data search root. The unsafe-path check examines the still-encoded resource_name, but the filesystem branch subsequently calls url2pathname(resource_name), so percent escapes such as %2e%2e become .. only after validation. os.path.join(path_, '../...') then resolves outside path_; os.path.exists() accepts the escaped target, find() returns a FileSystemPathPointer, and load()/open() reads the arbitrary process-readable file. In 3.9.4 the central path sentinel is reached, but ENFORCE=False only emits a warning and still calls builtins.open, so it does not close the read.

That is the smallest commit that first added percent-decoding before filesystem access and thereby made encoded traversal components active. Later raw-string path checks exposed the decode-after-check ordering, but did not originate the vulnerable decoding mechanism.

Direct parent-tree comparison `git diff e8c09039f8d805437a6fea14a3bce619db452eee 51ceb7517237d78b843a95db56629b11d41ede2b -- nltk/data.py` proves immediate-parent absence: the parent has `p = os.path.join(path_, resource_name)`, while the BIC first has `p = os.path.join(path_, url2pathname(resource_name))` (and likewise adds decoding for the zipfile component). A Python stdlib check produced `url2pathname('%2e%2e/SECRET_credentials.txt') == '../SECRET_credentials.txt'`.

`git cat-file -p 51ceb7517237d78b843a95db56629b11d41ede2b` shows parent e8c09039f8d805437a6fea14a3bce619db452eee, author/committer Steven Xu, the Windows-path message, and no trailers or AI/bot identity. The BIC is an ordinary single-parent commit, not a squash or merge requiring decomposition.

The advisory-linked PR #3522 merged as aec4fce1b84ad725b8975f7365b23a4f626572a9 and routed FileSystemPathPointer.open() through nltk.pathsec, but that merge is already reachable from tag 3.9.4 and its nltk/pathsec.py sets `ENFORCE = False`; validation only warns and permits builtins.open, so it is preparatory mitigation rather than the effective version-boundary fix.

audit_record.flaw_origin: Commit 51ceb7517237d78b843a95db56629b11d41ede2b made a Windows compatibility change in nltk/data.py: it imported url2pathname and changed the ordinary-filesystem join from os.path.join(path_, resource_name) to os.path.join(path_, url2pathname(resource_name)). Later raw-string path checks exposed the decode-after-check ordering, but did not originate the vulnerable decoding mechanism.

causal_chain.bug_semantics: OpenAM 16.0.6 installs the iPlanetDirectoryPro SSO cookie with com.sun.identity.cookie.httponly=false and com.iplanet.am.cookie.secure=false and without a SameSite default. Its OAuth2/OIDC consent path also exposed that same session identifier to JavaScript and treated it as the csrf form value. Consequently, same-origin script execution could read and replay the bearer session, and could satisfy the consent check with the stolen session identifier; the missing SameSite and protocol-derived Secure defaults widened cross-site and transport exposure.
causal_chain.flaw_origin: The smallest non-move commit that first wrote the advisory-specific SSO-token-as-CSRF mechanism is 4f04731207681973251c52436f07118e7c325e88. It created openam-oauth2/src/main/java/org/forgerock/oauth2/core/CsrfProtection.java with ssoToken.getTokenID().toString() as the expected csrf value, created OAuth2ConsentPageHelper.js to read the configured SSO cookie through CookieHelper.getCookie, and changed main-authorize.js to submit that value. Earlier insecure cookie defaults existed in the migrated codebase, but their first appearances in this Git history are copy/move imports and therefore are not valid BICs under the protocol; 4f04731207681973251c52436f07118e7c325e88 is the first reconstructable direct commit that completed the consent-specific vulnerable coupling removed by the patch.

causal_chain.bug_semantics: The authenticated chat-user endpoint accepts q after only trimming it and requiring two characters, then Chat::searchUsers() applies the database driver's ordinary SQL-string escape and interpolates the result into LOWER(ud.display_name) LIKE '%%%s%%'. SQL-string escaping prevents a quote breakout but leaves the LIKE pattern metacharacters % and _ active. Thus q=%% or q=__ passes the length gate and broadens the predicate instead of searching for those literal characters, letting any logged-in user retrieve active users' IDs and display names and systematically enumerate accounts.
causal_chain.flaw_origin: Commit a7275859a5d6bc19c20827fe1ec6f6d925ea6f27 introduced the chat feature, the authenticated user-search controller, and Chat::searchUsers() together. causal_chain.bug_semantics: An administrator-controlled RSE creation request can persist HTML/JavaScript in the city, country_name, or ISP metadata fields. The WebUI then treats those stored strings as markup in two victim-facing paths: lib/rucio/web/ui/static/rses.js passes the raw API objects directly to DataTables columns, and lib/rucio/web/ui/static/rse.js concatenates metadata values into HTML passed to jQuery.append. Loading the RSE Management list or an RSE detail page therefore executes the stored payload in the viewer's WebUI origin, where it can read JavaScript-accessible session/token material and act with the victim's authority.
causal_chain.flaw_origin: Commit 8f1a24a568331b10f9d8fb099ef233af340b7735 introduced the RSE-management WebUI feature as one ordinary commit. It added the create form and POST client for raw city/country_name/ISP values, the /rse, /rses, and /rses/add UI routes, the listing DataTable whose data source is the unencoded server response, and the detail-table helper that interpolates returned values into HTML. The persistence API predated or existed independently of the browser view, but this commit first created the executable rendering sinks and the documented WebUI create/trigger lifecycle.

causal_chain.bug_semantics: An attacker who can add an account identity can POST an identity string containing HTML or JavaScript to /accounts/<account>/identities. The backend stores that identity string and the account-identities GET endpoint returns it. On the WebUI account page, load_identities handed the returned objects directly to jQuery DataTables as data and selected the identity and type properties as columns. DataTables treated those string values as cell HTML, so merely viewing the affected account page inserted the persisted identity into the DOM and executed attacker-controlled script in the viewer's WebUI origin.
causal_chain.flaw_origin: Commit 4f67434304e5bd445c01a636d88113b76a68ef78 created the account-administration page and lib/rucio/web/ui/static/account.js. Its new load_identities function passed the server response directly to DataTable with `data: data` and `columns: [{'data': 'identity'}, {'data': 'type'}]`, without encoding the identity before the HTML sink. The same feature commit also added the UI's identity-creation helper, completing the store-and-render path. The pre-existing backend identity model/API stored and returned the supplied identity as data; the vulnerability began when this commit added the unsafe browser rendering, not when later code was moved or refactored.

causal_chain.bug_semantics: The Elasticsearch, OpenSearch, and GemFire vector-store converters serialize a caller-supplied Filter.Key into a Lucene-style query string. Their escaping left tab, LF, CR, and U+3000 ideographic space unescaped, so a key can introduce token boundaries and operators such as OR; the resulting string is passed to the backend query parser, allowing an attacker to replace the intended metadata predicate with arbitrary query clauses.
causal_chain.flaw_origin: Commit 9334d7d540f8d0ee7cb09e44b272c95c2c159627 first added an affected backend and the causal pattern: ElasticsearchAiSearchFilterExpressionConverter.doKey() appended the metadata-prefixed Filter.Key directly to the query string with only trim(), while ElasticsearchVectorStore supplied that converted string to Elasticsearch queryString(). OpenSearch later copied the affected converter in 46e47849cec4b8a6fffbd13997f3cce4f886347b, and GemFire added the same kind of filter-query path in 833a856f51090f0eb98332db2341ce7a107af1fd. Later shared-converter refactors and partial escaping changed the location and reduced the character set but did not create the vulnerability or close the whitespace bypass.

causal_chain.bug_semantics: The authenticated /v1/completions endpoint accepted an outer list of text prompts or token-id prompts of attacker-chosen length. The serving path treated every outer-list element as a separate prompt, eagerly created one engine generator per element, merged all generators, and allocated per-prompt response state, so a single bounded-size HTTP control action could fan out into unbounded CPU, memory, scheduling, and engine-request work before any aggregate prompt-count budget was enforced.
causal_chain.flaw_origin: PR #2529 deliberately added batch completion support. Its first member commit d04fd49c2bc9540237d3d11b6d1de26bbc35d232 removed the immediate-parent guard that rejected len(prompts) > 1 and replaced the single engine.generate call with an unbounded for-loop over prompts, a generators list, merge_async_iterators(*generators), and response arrays sized by len(prompts), without adding an outer prompt-count limit. The second member only added type hints; squash landing 3a7dd7e367277c47472912e84375fa912df07328 preserved the flawed mechanism.

causal_chain.bug_semantics: PickleScan classified a pickle only from GLOBAL/INST/STACK_GLOBAL module-and-name references found in its opcode stream. A malicious pickle could import the unblocked pkgutil.resolve_name, call it by REDUCE with data such as 'os:system' to obtain a blocked callable without importing that callable, then invoke the returned callable with a second REDUCE. Because REDUCE arguments and returned stack values were not resolved into new globals, the scanner saw only pkgutil.resolve_name and reported no dangerous global while unpickling executed arbitrary code.
causal_chain.flaw_origin: Commit c1d5abdcc740e0d08a0d12d015d08e1e6f29a67e created the scanner, its finite _suspicious_globals blocklist, the _list_globals routine that extracts only direct GLOBAL and STACK_GLOBAL references, and scan_pickle_bytes' table-membership decision. That initial design first made indirect callable resolution through an unlisted resolver such as pkgutil.resolve_name invisible; later table growth retained the same flaw until pkgutil.resolve_name was explicitly blocked.

causal_chain.bug_semantics: An authenticated attacker can submit a replication rule whose persisted comment contains HTML or script. The rule-detail page fetched all rule metadata and concatenated every returned key and value into a jQuery-created HTML row before appending it to #t_metadata; therefore the returned comments value was parsed as markup and executed in the WebUI origin when a user opened /ui/rule. The approval page independently passed the unescaped comments property to DataTables, giving administrators a second stored-XSS trigger while reviewing pending rules.

Commit cebd5b059e8c4629a3ae0b2eccfd922ab906ebd7 later added the persisted rule comment field to the already-unsafe metadata path, and commit 010746bc16b72313d1e779fa9a15996c44b40a9f later added the separate raw-comments DataTables sink on approve_rules.js. The original 2014 sink, rather than either later source-enablement or sink-copy commit, is the smallest commit that first wrote the vulnerable rendering mechanism.

causal_chain.bug_semantics: The MCP-exposed ado installer accepted an attacker-controlled package name and interpolated it into executable Stata source without validation or quoting. A package containing a newline therefore terminated the intended `ssc install` command and introduced another Stata command; Stata's `shell`/`!` escape then executed an arbitrary OS command with the server process's privileges. In the advisory-era implementation, `ado_package_install` forwarded `package` through `SSC_Install.install()` to `StataController.run()`/`pexpect.sendline()`; in the original implementation, the same untrusted value was written into a `.do` file and that file was executed by Stata.
causal_chain.flaw_origin: b61cd574b86bb6aa3a931ed637de0fb66ce82607 first added the MCP tool `ssc_install(command, is_replace)` in `src/stata_mcp/__init__.py`: lines 646-650 interpolated `command` directly into `write_dofile(f"ssc install {command}...")` and immediately passed the resulting file to `stata_do`. The immediate parent had no SSC-install tool or SSC command construction. Later commits moved the server code and replaced this implementation with the `ado_package_install(package)`/`SSC_Install.install(package)` framework, preserving the same missing trust-boundary validation rather than originating it.

`git log --all --reverse -S'ssc install {command}' -- '*.py'` led to b61cd574b86bb6aa3a931ed637de0fb66ce82607. Its patch adds the complete `ssc_install` MCP tool. At that tree, `src/stata_mcp/__init__.py:630-650` exposes attacker-controlled `command`, interpolates it into `ssc install` source, writes the source to a do-file, and calls `stata_do`; lines 690-699 construct `StataDo` and execute that file.

Direct parent verification: `git grep -n -E 'ssc_install|ssc install \{|ssc install' 9ef0a4076b51955786a29afc7de4bb1c782b6faf -- src` returned no matches. Thus neither the vulnerable MCP entry point nor its SSC command construction exists in the immediate parent tree.

These preserve/refactor the flaw first introduced by b61cd574b86bb6aa3a931ed637de0fb66ce82607, so none is the BIC.

Its added tests explicitly reject a newline-bearing `regress\nshell` value. Follow-on hardening 1641e93a71e7d1600adb2c7ab1041370d43347d4 and 7a00a338f0efd2c9b186a3923e6b56d8828db804 retained validation and added confirmation/policy changes, but b2bc49ec447836e0b1d442ece472c42b7f78724b is the first direct fix for this injection.

causal_chain.bug_semantics: Legacy PyTorch serialization unpickles the first pickle to obtain MAGIC_NUMBER, so that value may be computed by a REDUCE callable rather than encoded as an INT/LONG opcode. picklescan's get_magic_number instead disassembled the first pickle and returned only the first opcode whose name contained INT or LONG. An attacker could encode eval('0x1950A86A20F9469CFC6C') as the first pickle: PyTorch obtains the correct magic number, while picklescan obtains None and rejects/abandons the PyTorch scan before examining the later pickle containing the dangerous payload. The file therefore remains loadable by PyTorch while the scanner misses the code-execution globals.
causal_chain.flaw_origin: Commit f98f9bd89b16ab1b1b1b6366acddd1b2a4d36fe9 introduced old-format PyTorch scanning and, in the same focused commit, created src/picklescan/torch.py:get_magic_number with the literal INT/LONG-opcode heuristic and src/picklescan/scanner.py:scan_pytorch with the pre-scan magic-number rejection. Its immediate parent had neither torch.py nor scan_pytorch, so this is the smallest original commit that wrote the flawed semantic approximation; later cursor, exception-handling, routing, and logging changes retained rather than originated it.

The advisory declares affected versions <1.0.3 and patched version 1.0.3.

A targeted standard-library reproduction of the first pickle produced opcodes PROTO, GLOBAL, BINPUT, BINUNICODE, BINPUT, TUPLE1, BINPUT, REDUCE, BINPUT, STOP. Applying the historical `"INT" in opcode.name or "LONG" in opcode.name` extraction returned None, while pickle.loads returned 119547037146038801333356, exactly 0x1950A86A20F9469CFC6C. causal_chain.bug_semantics: An unauthenticated WebUI userpass login first resolves the submitted username to an account. A username with no mapping returns an account/identity-not-found page, while a mapped username with a wrong password proceeds to token authentication and returns a different token/authentication failure page. The response content therefore reveals whether the submitted username exists.

Later refactors made the text more explicit and ported the same branch structure to Flask, but did not originate the observable discrepancy.

causal_chain.bug_semantics: A pickle GLOBAL/STACK_GLOBAL for the module-level callable profile.run is parsed as module="profile", name="run". PickleScan classified a global as an issue only when the module appeared in its manually enumerated unsafe map and the extracted name exactly matched that module's filter (or the filter was "*"). The original map omitted profile entirely; a later attempted hardening used {"Profile.run", "Profile.runctx"}, which still could not match the extracted module-level names "run" and "runctx". Thus a malicious pickle could produce zero issues and then profile.run(statement) would reach Profile.run and exec(statement) when unpickled.
causal_chain.flaw_origin: The flaw originated in the first PickleScan implementation: it introduced an exact-name, manually enumerated dangerous-global filter without any entry for Python's profile module. That made profile.run executable but undetected from the scanner's first release lineage. Commit aecd11be98702caa9ba9b12189d91ad596a36114 later added class-qualified profile names, but it was not the BIC because its immediate parent already allowed the same module-level profile.run payload; it only preserved the pre-existing omission as a name-shape mismatch.

causal_chain.bug_semantics: ChaiScript's built-in async() launched a script closure with std::async(std::launch::async, ...) but did not make the Dispatch_Engine own or join the worker. During engine teardown, an outstanding script worker could continue formatting an eval_error and call Dispatch_Engine::get_type_name and Type_Info::bare_equal while the main thread destroyed the engine's type maps, producing a race-dependent heap use-after-free.

Later edits only adjusted registration syntax, module passing, namespaces, or formatting while retaining the same untracked launch.

causal_chain.bug_semantics: The optimized standard integer for-loop exposed its stack-local C++ counter to ChaiScript with var(&i). ChaiScript's intentional := reference-assignment could therefore copy an alias to that counter into a returned Boxed_Value. Once the compiled loop lambda returned, the counter's stack lifetime ended, but an escaping value (including one transported through async/future) retained the raw pointer; interpolation then reached Boxed_Number::get_as and dereferenced dangling storage, producing garbage, an invalid read, or a segmentation fault.
causal_chain.flaw_origin: Commit 683164650a462b6d5ea58bb899f4c2e668243a1d introduced the compiled-for-loop fast path and, within that new path, created int i on the lambda stack and registered var(&i). The existing reference-assignment semantics made the new stack-backed binding escapable. Later optimizer extraction and formatting commits only moved or reformatted this mechanism. The fix instead places the counter in an owning Boxed_Value and obtains the native int reference from that owned storage, so escaping aliases retain the allocation.

causal_chain.bug_semantics: The script-visible async() function launched std::async(std::launch::async, t_func) without making the spawned work part of the ChaiScript engine's lifetime. A script could finish while async functions were still evaluating identifiers against Dispatch_Engine maps; engine teardown then freed those map nodes, and a worker's subsequent lookup compared a freed std::string key in chaiscript::str_less::operator(), producing a heap use-after-free.
causal_chain.flaw_origin: Commit 52d03a66b15358e8fd2caeb5b063044c8aa839d2 first registered the ChaiScript async() API in include/chaiscript/chaiscript_stdlib.hpp and returned an independently executing std::future, but introduced no engine-owned thread tracking or destructor join. Later commits only adjusted registration syntax, module ownership, bootstrap qualification, and formatting while preserving that lifetime mismatch until the 2026 fix.

causal_chain.bug_semantics: The unauthenticated Genkit developer Tools server accepted action-execution requests while listening beyond a loopback-only trust boundary and did not validate the HTTP Host header. CORS only controls which origins receive browser-readable response headers; it does not stop the handler, and a DNS-rebound page retains its attacker origin while resolving its hostname to the developer machine. Consequently a LAN client or DNS-rebound browser could reach the action runner, supply an action key and input (later also context), execute any registered flow/tool/model/prompt, and read the returned result. The reported chain also used the telemetry SSE endpoint's wildcard Access-Control-Allow-Origin to read trace inputs and outputs.
causal_chain.flaw_origin: The earliest persisted tree that makes the network-listening Runner API actually execute actions is squash aggregate 91ed3de52e7db92943886526395ad8eac6faa77f: it adds genkit-tools/src/runner/router.ts with a runAction mutation that proxies to the reflection server and changes genkit-tools/src/runner/runner.ts to expose that router through api.listen(port) without a host argument or Host validation. Its parent 805600159f34ca96d95c26c10c7b2799cb5951ce already had the all-interface Express listener but only stubbed, NOT_IMPLEMENTED flow operations, so it lacked the action-execution primitive. The squash message lists many member commits, including the causally relevant 'Implemented passthrough endpoints in Runner API', but that member commit object and SHA are not retained in the validated clone or associated public PR history; therefore the protocol's smallest non-aggregate BIC cannot be named.

causal_chain.bug_semantics: Command_OPEN_POWERSHELL took the directory of the file being edited and interpolated it verbatim into the PowerShell program -NoExit -Command "Set-Location -Path '<directory>'". A Windows directory name may contain a single quote, so an attacker-controlled directory can terminate the PowerShell single-quoted literal and append PowerShell statements. When a victim opens a file from that directory and invokes Open PowerShell/Open Terminal (including the administrator variant), ShellExecuteW starts powershell.exe and executes the injected statements with the victim's privileges.

causal_chain.bug_semantics: An unauthenticated Core-protocol connection could send a FEDERATION_DOWNSTREAM_CONNECT packet on the federation channel. CoreProtocolManager installed LocalChannelHandler on that channel and handled the packet without first requiring an authenticated Subject or an authorized federation-deployment role; it accepted the attacker's connector, credentials, policies, and transformers, constructed an upstream federation configuration, and called FederationManager.deploy. The target broker would therefore initiate an outbound Core federation connection to the attacker's rogue broker, enabling queue-message injection or exfiltration when inbound Core and outbound connectivity were both available.
causal_chain.flaw_origin: The missing-authentication mechanism originated in fb54707e2db9a6308e53a6be7f45b66129eb225f (ARTEMIS-2549), the one-commit downstream-federation feature change. The direct parent lacked both the packet constant use and FederationDownstreamConnectMessage class.

causal_chain.bug_semantics: RustCrypto ml-dsa signature decoding used one monotonic() predicate for two different encodings. Hint cut offsets may repeat because an ML-DSA polynomial may contain no hints, but hint indices within each polynomial must be strictly increasing. Changing the shared predicate from < to <= made cuts valid but also accepted equal adjacent indices. A verifier therefore decoded a non-canonical signature containing a repeated hint index and could accept a byte-distinct malleation of a valid signature.

Wycheproof later supplied invalid repeated-hint vectors that exposed the regression.

causal_chain.bug_semantics: An authenticated board editor could send a single-block or batch PATCH naming a comment block created by another member. The handlers checked only the caller's general ability to manage board cards and the target block's board, then applied the caller-controlled patch; they never enforced comment ownership or the elevated permission for acting on other users' comments. causal_chain.bug_semantics: A STOMP client authenticated with only SEND or CONSUME permission could request a routing type that an existing address did not support. STOMP's auto-create path added that routing type by calling the broker server's updateAddressInfo directly, without the ServerSession CREATE_ADDRESS authorization check; the subsequent routing-semantics check then observed the newly added type and accepted the send or subscription. This let a low-privilege user mutate address routing configuration despite lacking createAddress permission.
causal_chain.flaw_origin: Commit d773e8f66b5db2b0fcaa646384c24690d38aaa69 added the first existing-address/missing-routing-type branch to StompConnection.autoCreateDestinationIfPossible. It copied the address's routing types, added the client-requested effectiveAddressRoutingType, and invoked manager.getServer().updateAddressInfo(...) directly. The parent only auto-created through the authenticated ServerSession when an address did not exist and otherwise left an unsupported routing type for checkRoutingSemantics to reject. Later edits moved or modernized the same sink but did not originate the authorization bypass.
